utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Hendriks, before we continue, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Kuzmanovic, you asked the witness to prepare a list of documents he solely authored at the time. Mr. Kuzmanovic, we have considered whether we would encourage the witness to do so. Over the weekend, we have looked at the correspondence between ECMM and the Chamber, and we thought that could be done safely without in any way interfering with the reasons why the documents were redacted; however, Mr. Hendriks has prepared a list but has not limited himself to shows documents he solely prepared himself. So, therefore, I suggest -- I take it that the reason why you'd need that is just to know better how to cross-examined, rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, one of the problems is that on the list Mr. Hendriks has prepared, we find more than just his own name. So, therefore, I'm afraid that we have to redact this list again, so it exclusively provides you with the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know the specific ones that he has written that were not redacted, and that is 812 -- and I can go through that list now, Your Honour, because I had that list already: P812 - these are all P numbers by the way - 814, 818, 945, and 957. The other documents -- and I did get a call from Chambers, and I appreciated the assistance that I received from Chambers. We went over the remaining documents, and those were the documents either that were -- that were all redacted, which I was not sure whether he wrote them himself or he -- or the witness co-authored him. And those were the ones I was looking for, Your Honour. Make we could ask the witness, or if he has provided that to Chambers, that would be a route to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the problem is he provided them in such a way that sometimes when he was not the sole author, it, nevertheless, appears on the list and also names the other person who authored that. So we have to -- I'll ask Ms. van den Berge to perhaps take out again those documents from the list that are not authored solely by Mr. Hendriks, and then provide it to you. Would that be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That would be wonderful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, you'll receive a list, although a very short list of documents, solely authored by Mr. Hendriks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, thank you, first of all, for doing your homework during the weekend. Thank you for that. Mr. Kuzmanovic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hendriks, for reviewing those documents. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before getting into those documents, I wanted to pull up 65 ter 2410, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, that's your statement of April 18th, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we go to page 2 of that statement, please. Page 2 of the statement itself, not the second page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This statement, Mr. Hendriks, was not part of your -- not part of your -- I'm sorry. This statement was not discussed in your direct examination, Mr. Hendriks. We talked about it briefly on Friday. The first part of your statement here, at the stop of page 2, discusses that it was your impression that the Croats were able to take over the Krajina within two days, and you listed several reasons, the first being that Operation Storm was well prepared and executed on an unexpected day. When you say "Operation Storm was well prepared and executed," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly as it reads, such an Operation Storm only has a chance of successful if it is well prepared and carried out accordingly, so rapidly and smart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that rapidly and smart is an assessment that you made based on your observations, but what were the specific things that made it rapid and smart?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't elaborate too much on that because I wasn't present. I was in a bunker and was unable to observe anything. But the mere fact that it was finished within a day was cause for me to say they managed to take care of that quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, your second point was the ARSK was not well equipped and organised. Was that based on your observations when you were in Sector South, before Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because, in effect, we were not allowed to observe the ARSK lines; but, later on, we saw basically what they looked like and we concluded that -- well, that distribution was not that rock-solid --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The defence was not that rock-solid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any indication that there was mobilisation called at the end of July of 1995, of all able-bodied mean in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because among others, my interpreter's friend was mobilised. So it was said that all able-bodied men were mobilised at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Point number 4 on this document, sir, says: "Most of the ARSK defence forces pulled out after the recommendation of the Krajina authorities (by radio Knin) to the population to flee asap." Now, was it your understanding that Radio Knin was broadcasting an evacuation of the population out of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly how it worked. That is what I heard from my interpreter who also had that from hearsay, and that is about how it must have gone. So I can't be clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just to make -- just to clarify that a little bit, it's your understanding that you learned from your interpreter that Radio Knin was broadcasting an evacuation of the local population. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that through my interpreter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of your interpreter?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two. I know only their first names: Renata and Sandra.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Later on, in page two of your document at the very bottom, you say: "The Croats didn't want to destroy the main cities because they would like to populated them asap with all the DPs ..." I'm assuming that's displaced persons. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I see you're nodding your head. DPs is displaced persons, correct? Yes?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "... from the coastal areas." Now, where did you get the information that the Croats didn't want to destroy the main cities?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was, in effect, a conclusion we reached on our own because Knin was not destroyed and other large cities were not destroyed, so the Croats had that problem with displaced persons and got back to that later on. So we didn't hear from -- we didn't hear about that from somebody else, that was our own conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: On the next page of your statement, page 3, at the very top, it says: "To the assessment of General Forand, the commander of UN Sector South, the pause of the shelling could have been a deal between Tudjman and Milosevic in order to prevent a slaughtering by giving the opportunity to the population to flee away to Bosnia/Serbia." Now, was this something that you heard directly from General Forand?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that directly, but I do know that General Forand wrote his own account of the Operation Storm situation and his conclusions on that subject; and I believe that this was the subject we spoke about. So, in effect, that was his conclusion about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't have any indication that that occurred, meaning a deal between Tudjman and Milosevic, did you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but I can imagine it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, later on, in that paragraph, there's also some speculation about "the new RS general," who joined the ARSK forces a short time before Storm, "played a big role in breaking the resistance of the army by advising the commanders not to resist, but to save as much lives as possible." Where did you get the information that led you to that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe from that same summary by General Forand, but I can't say that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Just so I'm clear, the assessment that you make, based on what you thought was something that came from General Forand, is that the new general essentially broke the will of his own military to resist?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not so much the will to resist as the will to indicate at a certain point: "Men, don't let massive slaughter happen, get out of here in time." Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, your statement specifically says that this new RS general played a big role in breaking the resistance of the army. And by "army," we're talking the RSK army, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. If he is going to put the statement of the witness, he should be accurate in telling that the statement says that "it might be," not that it was stated as a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think the question is very simple and spoke for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the context is clear enough that it is a possibility which is described, "it might be." I have another question on my mind: The new RS general, who is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that perhaps General Mrksic? Does that name ring a bell to you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Getting back to my earlier question, your statement specifically says: "The new RS general played a big role in breaking the resistance of the army ..." My question to you is: The army was the RSK army, correct? He is referring to his own military?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So, again, I'll ask you: The conclusion here is that the RSK general broke the resistance of his own army?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That question was asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was asked, and not only that, but then the witness explained exactly what he meant by those words. Let's not make it -- he said "a massive" and "then get out." He has --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, in this paragraph -- or in this statement on this page, sir, in the paragraph which begins: "If the authorities ..." About the eighth line down, there's a sentence that says: "The absence of responses to requests for the results of investigations into numerous killings reported by UNCIVPOL, and then it says: "Figure until 3rd October 1995, 84 ... and the lack of patrols in the remote areas in order to stop the incidents underlines the attitude of the authorities." Now, I have several questions regarding that portion of your statement. The Croatian police had no obligation to report anything about results of investigations to UNCIVPOL, did it, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether or not they had such an obligation; but if UNCIVPOL had asked about that, apparently they didn't receive satisfactory answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you, yourself, don't know what kind of investigations were undertaken by the Croatian police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Meaning my statement is correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you don't know how many people may have been arrested or how many people may have been tried, or convicted, or acquitted. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Further down in this same statement, the next line says: "I think that the authorities must have been able to prevent most of the criminalities by sending out 'flying patrols' and by arresting, followed by punishment, the criminals." My first question to you is what is a "flying patrol"?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You shouldn't take it literally as it reads here, but simply a patrol that goes through the area here and there, not along a regular route but at random so that's not expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you say in the -- further in this sentence: "By arresting, followed by punishment." Is it your assertion that people should be arrested and punished without any kind of judicial process involved?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't mean it that way. There should always be a judicial process involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And, simply, if someone is arrested doesn't necessarily mean that they have to be punished if they're not convicted. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the judge decides that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to move 65 ter 2410 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the whole of the statement, Mr. Kuzmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Has an attestation been given on the whole of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that is the appropriate way because it would then be, more or less, a 92 ter statement, unless you would want to limit it to one way to the portions read, but then there is no need to tender it, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I do want to tender it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, fine then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I could go through it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we know whether the witness had an opportunity to review this statement? Mr. Hendriks, did you recently have a look at this document and were you able to review whether it accurately states what you said at the time, or haven't you seen it for a while?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean my statement from 1996, Your Honour? I did, in fact, re-read it last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you re-read it last week, did you find it an accurate reflection of the statement you gave in 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because it's 13 years later now, and I don't have any reason to take a different view of things. I set it forth in writing at that time as I felt about it then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So may I understand your last answer to be that you gave that statement at that time, to the best of your recollection, in accordance with the truth and that would you not give any answers different from the answers given at that time, if you would be asked the same questions today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is it's own story. It's just -- it's not based on any standard list of questions, other than what I wrote in the document at that time; and, at that time, that was my truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you still consider this statement to be the truth, to the best of your recollection, today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that this would be the attestation we would need under Rule 92 ter. Mr. Hedaraly, you have no problem with that? Then, Mr. Registrar, could you please assign a number to the 1996 statement, or rather, written report by Mr. Hendriks.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D820.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D820 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, you were kind enough to review many of these ECMM reports over the weekend to determine, other than the ones that were identified, which of the redacted reports you had written exclusively, and I will briefly like to go through those with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: P951, if that could be called up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, this is a document dated September 9th of 1995, and it is entitled "Special report of the condition of cultural heritage in former Krajina." I believe you were asked some questions generally about this in your direct examination, if I'm not mistaken. You do mention in a number of instances, for example, in Cetina, in Vrlika, and in -- excuse me, Biskupija, the specific -- and Milosi, the specific type of church, whether it is Catholic or Orthodox, whether it was damaged or intact. But for the most part, in this report, there is not a designation of which church, whether Catholic or Orthodox, was touched or untouched, damaged or undamaged. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any specific reason, as far as you know, that you did not, other than those few instance, designate the type of church, whether it was an Orthodox church or a Catholic church, was damaged or undamaged?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's perfectly possible that at that time we didn't know exactly what type of church it was, so I didn't -- I didn't associate a specific designation with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The next redacted document that you said you had written yourself was P955.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If that could be pulled up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's a document dated September 7th. On the second page of the document, you note, toward the bottom of the document, that there's a Serbian gentleman who had a Croatian friend, and the comment is: "The Croatian friend said that the looting can't be prevented because this revenge can't be stopped in a 'country in war,' where no proper law and order is present." Now, the assessment of the friend of this Serbian gentleman, what caused you to put that in your report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A team comment has same value as the writer attributes to it. In effect, that was my reflection at the time that if even in Croatia people don't really believe in having order there, what should we believe in then? In other words, he made it appear as if it was simply something you would have to get used to; and, on that day, it surfaced in my mind as something that I wanted to set forth in writing. That's my opinion, and the higher echelons should do with that as they please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: But the looting and killing at some point did stop, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. I was in that area until the end of October; and, when I left, the looting and killing had not really stopped yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So it's your assessment that at the end of October of 1995, the looting and killing had not stopped at all?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anymore. I would need to review reports from that period. But as far as I remember, it had not stopped yet when I left the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The other report that you had written yourself is 65 ter 5475. This is a report dated August 2nd, 1995. This is before Operation Storm. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You note, in the middle of this paragraph, which is point number 2: "At the KenBat," meaning Kenyan Battalion, "meeting, we heard that with RSK shelled the area of Strmica-Grahovo at least 50 times with artillery, and that they now have taken their positions and that they are trying to solve the supply problems." Now, before Operation Storm, according to your report, the RSK was shelling the area of Strmica to Grahovo. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reads that according to the Kenyan battalion that had bombed the RSK, and that's what I reflected, but I'm not sure whether it was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, wasn't that part and parcel of the RSK's position, to try to counterattack to retake Bosansko Grahovo that had fallen to the Croatian military?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly what the situation was because that was not the area of our interest, but we did try to gain an impression of what was taking place there. But whether the artillery had been by the with RSK, it can also be a misperception by the Kenyan battalion because there was no actual investigation as to who fired the artillery and where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, I didn't intervene before the witness answered the question, but if you ask about a report and if the witness says, "Well, that's what they said, but whether it is true or not," then the next question to see, "wouldn't that part and parcel of ..." So, of course, if the witness doesn't know whether it happened at all, to ask him to put in an certain context something he says he doesn't whether know is true or not is not something that greatly assists the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, happily enough, in the answer, the witness could explain. It is very difficult for him to answer a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. What is puzzling to me, though, is whenever there is an indication of the RSK shelling or committing some act, he doesn't know, but whenever there is some allegation about the Croats doing something, all of a sudden it becomes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is inappropriate comment, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's one. Second, there is an reason here, because RSK is here put between, how do you call it, not brackets but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- quotation marks. Therefore, I find, first of all, that in this specific instance, that there is a reason in the written report for the answers the witness gave. Whether they're correct or not, of course I have no judgement on that at this moment. But you should refrain from --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- from telling that this witness gives answers in such-and-such direction. I take that the apologies are directed to Mr. Hendriks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move 65 ter 5475 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D821, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D821 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go, please, to P952.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, I'm now going to move to ECMM reports, most of which have redacted authors, and these documents were documents that you indicated you were not the author of. But they have all been moved in through you, so I'm going to ask you some questions about a certain selection of them, just so you know. This is a report dated September 6th of 1995; and, on point 5, which is on the second page, the heading is "Economic, industrial, and infrastructure matters." Section a says: "43.000 people used to live before in 43 local communities of the Knin municipality, covering 1.079 square kilometres." Do you have any knowledge, Mr. Hendriks, as to where these particular figures were discovered or what the source of those figures is?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The reason I ask you that question is there -- there has been considerable testimony about the number of people in the Knin municipality and in Sector South that left before and during the course of Operation Storm. At least according to this ECMM document, the 43.000 people who used to live in these communities, there is no indication as to how many of those people stayed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure they figured out how many people lived there at the time and how many people were still present after Operation Storm has been estimated as well, but I couldn't tell you how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Later, in that same paragraph, it talks about: "Knin's commissioner's office having 453 flats under their supervision, but most of those people needing flats/houses or accommodation do not wish to move into houses of run-away Serbs." Now, at least according to this report, it appears as though displaced persons did not want to populate flats that had been abandoned by Serbs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it's stated there, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to P954, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report. While it's coming up, I'll give you the date of it, sir. It's September 11th of 1995. Point number 2, political matters, it says: "Team Gospic learned from the," and there's a redaction, "of the Lika-Senj Zupanje that this county has 3.700 square kilometres and 71.000 inhabitants." Now, it appears from this document - and please correct me if I'm wrong - that the 71.000 inhabitants referred to in this paragraph are people currently living in this zupanje, or county. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not draft this report. I assume that at the time there was a summary at CC level of what was known at the time. So I can't tell you exactly whether it was before or after that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Later in this document at the bottom, under military, operational and security matters, point b, it says: "UN reports 500 to 600 explosions heard during the Sunday," and then going on to the next page, "morning hours in the general area of Boricevac in direction of Bosnian border. After this shelling, the state of the alert in the Donji Lapac area is relaxed, but HV police troops are still deployed, manning check-points wearing helmets and flak-jackets." Now, do you know what the "HV police troops" is referred to in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It appears from this paragraph that there's some significant fighting on at or near the Bosnian border and near Donji Lapac, at least as of the date of this report of September 11th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's perfectly possible. I don't think that they simply wrote that in the report for no reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could, please, go to P932.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is another ECMM report that was admitted through you, Mr. Hendriks, obviously noting that you're not the author, dated August 23rd of 1995. And if we look at section 2.d, it says: "During a visit in Mogoric, Team Gospic learned from in the village deployed policemen that the reason for their presence is to secure the remaining Serbs and to receive those who are hiding in the woods." Then there's a comment: "The fact that these policemen are from one department north-east of Zagreb shows that their superiors are afraid to use domestic police for their tasks, fearing crimes and harassment being committed against Serbs." Now, do you know were in any domestic police available in the newly liberated areas?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, there may be a translation issue here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Should I shorten and repeat the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm intervening because it has been done twice, so I don't think that repeating the question -- yes. But, perhaps, we could seek clarification with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You used the expression "domestic police." Did you want to refer to the police that would be locally present?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understand. I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Domestic police" can be translated in several ways and that might cause a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will -- I know where you're coming from, Your Honour. I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, from the context of this paragraph, it's clear that police in this area of -- liberated Croatia were police from Zagreb. Now, Zagreb obviously is not in Sector South. The comment about the need for use of police from Zagreb apparently showing that certain superiors are afraid to use what is termed here "domestic police" is apparently an issue in the report. Now, domestic police - you can tell me if I'm wrong - within the context of this paragraph, that is police that were locally based. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, were you aware during the time that you were in Sector South, Mr. Hendriks, of any domestic police that were native to the areas that were liberated, having been established right after Operation Storm; or were most of these police forces brought in from outside the area, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the following page, under section 5, again, "Economic, industrial, and infrastructural matters," there's a notation that says: "For the first time -- the first time, after four years water from the Zrmanja river started flowing again to Zadar." Were you aware, prior to Operation Storm, that the water flow to the area of Zadar which was not occupied was interrupted?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not learn anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In section b, there's a discussion that this is an project to redistribute live stock to people, and there's a mention that says the person whose name is redacted "was concerned that the governmental returning plan enabling people to return as quickly as possible to their former homes can only work in large cities but not in small villages or hamlets." Now, what I wanted to ask you about was the redistribution of live stock. There have been several indications throughout the course of this trial and in reports that livestock were being taken away by either civilians or members of the Croatian military. Now, it appears, at least by this report, that livestock was to be redistributed to people. Did you have any indication that livestock that you saw was being prepared for redistribution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The question in its form is fine, but I object to the commentary that led up to the question; that is, "there have been suggestion in this trial" and then he asks the question. If anything, it should have been done the other way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I fully agree with you that this is suggestive; but, of course, suggestive questions in cross-examination are not, as such, prohibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It is not the suggestion of the answer in the question, it is the suggestion that there is evidence in the trial before that has said something. It could be in misleading more than just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is an old issue. It certainly doesn't reflect the totality of the evidence we have received on the presence of livestock in the area and in what state they were. Nevertheless, it's also true that at least part of the evidence certainly reflects a system of redistribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question, Your Honour. I'll re-ask it. I don't think there is anything wrong with it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But perhaps if you would also put the question in such a way that -- I would know exactly what you were asking for because for me it would be very difficult to see whether a cow is prepared for redistribution if it's in a meadow, but, of course, there could be other situations which may be more clear. Please put the question again to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the context -- in the context of this particular paragraph, sir, there is a -- at least appeared to be a plan to redistribute livestock to people. Now, during your course of time that you were in Sector South, did you have any opportunity to observe what was being done with livestock and whether there was, in fact, any redistribution of livestock?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that I saw was that livestock was being loaded up by people. It could have been a systematic plan but livestock could also have been stolen or both processes could have taken place, but I don't have any genuine indications to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So, one or the other, you can't -- you don't know is a fair answer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to P933, please. You must have the wrong document here. It's 65 ter 30 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Kuzmanovic, your last question, where you said "you do not know whether it was the one or the other," that is, theft or redirect examination, by that question, did you aim at excludeing other possibilities?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I guess I did not. The question was one or the other, but I suppose there could be other possibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, a third, or a fourth or a fifth option, and owner. Someone owning cattle, loading up his cattle, and moving to another place would neither be redistribution or theft. What the witness said, I think, that he observed was people loading up cattle, that's all. So you did not intend to exclude other possibilities by the last question because, otherwise, we would have to put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. I did not exclude anything, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it may be clear from his observation that the factual observations of the witness apparently were that cattle was loaded and transported.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And beyond that, nothing else. Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The correct exhibit designation is P940. Mr. Registrar, I think that is 65 ter 3067, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that to come up, Mr. Hendriks, that's a report dated August 29th of 1995, and I'd like to go down to section e of number 3. Section e of number 3, says: "H-u-m-o." Could you tell me what that stands for, Humo?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Humanitarian officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It says: "Humanitarian officer reports that in Podinarje valley, nine RSK soldiers surrendered to HV under UN observation?" Then there is a comment: "As this joint action of UN/HV was successful, and the lifeline of Serb soldiers dwindles, we can expect an increasing number of surrenders." Now, were you aware that there were pockets of Serb soldiers in the mountains and woods of Sector South, similar to the ones that surrendered here?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is perfectly possible, but I can't be absolutely sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of any military activity that was ongoing in late August/early September 1995 to try to find these small pockets of ARSK soldiers that may be hiding in the mountains and woods?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to P934, please, and if we go to section 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It says, "Military, operational, and security matters." This is August 11th of 1995, and there is an notation here that says that: "The team was assured of complete FOM, freedom of movement, but was -- but advised them to remain on the main roads due to the ARSK snipers who remain in the hills. The team also met the chief of police in Gracac, Mr. Kavurin, who was busy setting up the policija station in town. They were, once again, assured of complete freedom of movement. Team reports much damage from shelling in the town, with many houses burnt, and a number of civilian protection forces men ..." I believe that should be "cleaning" the streets, not "leaning" the streets. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you -- did you happen to go to Gracac at any point in time around the 11th of August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably not, because this is about the Korenica team and that was the northern area and that was not our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to P935.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is an August 13th, 1995 report, and it discusses in the first section, political assessment, talking about the new mayor of Knin. It says in the first paragraph: "He is expected to be a puppet for the controlling Croat authorities and is purely a figurehead for the world to see how 'well' the remaining Serbs are being treated by the Croats." Now, can you give me any information upon what that assessment was based?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This report was compiled by the RC, and they had their own observations and conversations at that time. So that is their opinion that is reflected here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do understand that, Mr. Hendriks, and these document were admitted through you as a member of ECMM. So I guess I'm asking you as to whether or not had you any independent knowledge, other than what the authors in this report apparently said, about whether or not this new mayor of Knin was purely a figurehead. Do you have any information on your own regarding that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't feel that information is very valuable. When you talk to the men, you form an opinion; and, as I mentioned, this was written by the RC perhaps based on conversations or perhaps translation from a newspaper. It is a general story, it's a political assessment. So, whether or not he was a puppet, that is not for me, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have any interaction with that gentleman, the mayor of Knin?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of this particular document, there's a military assessment and analysis. It says, in the second sentence of that first paragraph: "It is assessed that the swiftness of the success of Operation Storm caught not only the HV by surprise but also the civilian authorities who were supposed to go in afterwards and take over. Consequently, as the 'capital' fell in 36 hours, instead of the expected week, the military and civilian police who were next to arrive did so late." Now, was it your experience that the Croatian government, based on your observations, was unprepared to deal with the situation because it happened so quickly in and around Knin?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The authorities in Knin had some difficulty getting it all off the ground. That was my observation. It was not pretty well prepared yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And it's true, is it not, that before Operation Storm occurred, the assessment was that the Croatian military would not be able to re-take -- the general assessment by Western observers, anyway, was that the Croatian military would not be able to retake the Sectors North and South. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The fact that it was taken within a short time caused quite a bit of chaos and unpreparedness on behalf of the Croatian government, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would need to ask them that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, based on -- do you agree with that -- with my statement, based upon what you observed during the course of time you were in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't simply state that cut and dry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. What can you state then? What do you mean by your answer?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The real cause of the chaos and whether the Croatian government was unprepared is impossible to tell. Perhaps, it was business as usual. On the other hand, things might have happened faster than expected and they didn't see it coming. I can't assess that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to section 3 of this same report, under "Humanitarian assessment."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, this as of August 13th of 1995. The first sentence of this says: "A well-planned and carefully executed clean-up operation has been in action throughout the week. The Croatian army and police have swept up through the former RSK, removing evidence." My question to you is: Removing evidence of what?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I mean, there was cleaning-up going on in and around Knin of the shops and the things that were smashed and broken, and the damage. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the implication at least is that there was something to hide by this statement?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you might say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yet the press and teams like the ECMM and the UNMOs and the HRAT team, they were all over Sector South during that time, were they not, as of August 13th of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, they were present, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: On the last page of this exhibit, sir, the second-last paragraph, the second sentence, it says: "Knin town and immediate surroundings have suffered only superficial damage and, therefore, are the only area where DPs can be expected to re-establish themselves. There appears to have been a specific policy to protect the town, as with the majority of Orthodox churches in the former Sector South." Now, was it your observation as well that Knin town and immediate surroundings suffered only superficial damage?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The town of Knin did, indeed, suffer superficial damage; but depending on what you consider to be the immediate surroundings, I would qualify that because as soon as you got outside Knin, there were a lot of burnt out houses and similar damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to P937, please, at the very bottom of that document, under 2, "Military assessment."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "In the former RSK ..." - again, this is 20th of August, 1995 - "... still an unknown number of Serb soldiers are fighting and hiding in the woods. The areas, according to UN and CALO, are Strmica, Mogoric, Mazin, and the wooden mountain range of Pljesevica (north Korenica). The HV tries with special anti-guerilla forces to catch these soldiers; but during their mopping actions, some HV solders were killed or caught by them. Also, in the Dinara area, some nests of ARSK soldiers are presumed, and so the HV authorities state that the whole country, not even Knin vicinity, is not 100 percent safe yet." My question to you regarding this military assessment is: Did you ever have an opportunity to observe these anti-guerilla forces in action; and in what areas, if so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the witness has answered the question. Nevertheless, part of the portion that was read to him by you does neither appear on the transcript, and approximately the same portions were not translated to him either due to your speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought I was going slow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you perhaps -- because in your question, you were talking about anti-guerilla forces and that is exactly, for example, the portion which was not read to him. I suggest that you read again now the whole of the portion at such a speed that the witness can hear the translation, that the transcribers are able to transcribe what you said, and that you then put the question again to the witness. He may come up with the same answer, but I would rather have a complete file on which he bases his answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will. Thank you, Your Honour thank. I will endeavor to read more slowly. Just so Your Honour knows, I have about three more reports to review after this, and then I will be done. So, if we need to go beyond the break, it will be very, very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you can could that, well, let's say, within the next ten minutes approximately then, we would have the break a little bit later, so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour, so I can finish, and I will do my best to read a little more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, you understand when you read English, do you not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to read this section 2, "Military assessment"? I know I read it to you, but you had a chance to review it on your screen. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if we invite the witness to read on from the top of this page, especially where it reads "the HV tries with ..." Could you please read that portion again, Mr. Hendriks, in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, I had asked you a question earlier about whether or not you had a chance to observe what's termed in this report "special anti-guerilla forces of the HV." Can you tell us, please, once again, whether or not you had a chance to observe them; and if so, when and where?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we can go to P939, please, which is an ECMM report dated August 27, 1995, we'll go to page 2, the bottom of page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Under section b, it says: "Operation Storm seems not to be finished yet due to the big number of police, special police, and HV monitored in the Srb, Donji Lapac, and Mazin area. Local commanders passed to UN and ECMM some unconfirmed information about small fighting between diminutive groups of ARSK soldiers hiding in the woods west of Srb and Donji Lapac, and HV and police forces ransacking the wooden terrain." Now, had you had an opportunity to go up into this area where these operations were going on, Srb, Donji Lapac, and Mazin?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, those areas were outside our patrol area, so that would have come from a different team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to P941, this is an August 31st ECMM report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, there's a mention in section 3, under "Military, operational, and security matters," that: "Team N2 was informed through a letter from General Cermak about ROM," restriction of movement, "in the widen areas north-east of Knin, stretching in to Bosansko Grahovo, in an area 20 by 20 kilometres. All IOs," meaning international organisations, "are prohibited to go there due to cleaning actions done by special police forces." Now, were you made aware of areas in which special -- mop-up activity was going on by special police forces?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Where was it made known to you that these mop-up activities by special police forces were occurring?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it says here, we saw a letter signed by General Cermak, but I don't remember where I saw that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever in any areas after mop-up operations had occurred?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, as we sit here today, what areas those might have been?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We drove throughout the entire South Sector in September. There were two or three teams that covered the South Sector. So that included the areas where the mop-up operations took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: But you, yourself, didn't observe what may or may not have happened after those mop-up operations took place, correct? You just drove through the areas where they occurred.

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I also spoke with people there, so our standard operating procedure of driving, visiting villages, talking to people, and listening to hear what had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: None of that specific information about what happened and who you spoke to after a mop-up operation is contained in any of the reports have you written. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The last document I'm going to go through with you, sir, is P958. It's dated the 12th of September of 1995, and section 2, "Political matters," the part b. It says: "The chief of police in Gospic," and then there's a redaction, "informed Team G-1 that, for the moment, coordination between police and other administrative authorities is not possible and that the police, as a lack of personnel, for effective control in the AOR," meaning Lika-Senj County. "The looting in the liberated areas is, according to him, the result of deep hate and revenge feeling. He stressed that ten policemen have already been fired because they committed criminal acts. "He also complained that police arrested thieves but justice does not react in a proper way. Chief of police explained the duties of the special police: Discover minefields and clear them, find hidden warehouses of ammunition, look for hidden people. "Finally, he said that Croatian leaders saw only problems to liberate the occupied area, but now they are faced with problems they have not expected before." And there are two questions I'd like it ask but that section that I just read to you. From what you saw and you observed during the course of time in Sector South, it is true, is it not, that the civilian authorities, based upon what was going on in Sector South, were not prepared to deal with the problems they were facing, specifically looting and burning. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the issue of the duties of the special police, as described by the chief of police in Gospic, did you ever observe the special police involved in any of the activities described here: Discovering, minefields, finding hidden warehouses of ammunition, and looking for hidden people?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any reason to disagree with the explanation of the role of the special police, at least as described here?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the account of the chief of police in Gospic, he said that; but, moreover, Gospic is not a mine area. That was stated to the Gospic team and they simply wrote that down, and I have no reason to say that that account is nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: One final question: Based on your observations in your area of responsibility, is it fair to state that, other than engaging in mop-up operations, you were not aware of what the role of the special police was?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very generally, we knew what the role was of the special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I guess -- other than mop-up operations, what did you observe the role of the special police was in your area of responsibility, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't observe any of that, but we did know what the purpose was of the special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I don't want to keep asking the same question. But what was the purpose, from your understanding, of the special police? You've told us that you knew what it was, but you haven't told us what it was.

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, tracing munitions warehouses, discovering minefields, and those types of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions. Thank you for the extra time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Kehoe, everything depended on what time the others would take, isn't it right, for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would expect in two hours, I finish, I do believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break, and we will resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the third cross-examining party always has the advantage, could also call it disadvantage, that part of the ground has already been covered by the others. In view of that, I'd like to encourage you to see whether you could do it in one hour and a half; and, of course, if you show that your questions are always focussed not too much art of advocacy, just the advocacy in itself would do, I would say. And, of course, if you proceed in that way, we see that could you not conclude within that one and a half hour. We would give you additional time, but take the advantage of part of the ground already been covered by the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe, and Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hendriks. I will try not to cover ground that has been covered before, but I will bounce between some of the things in your statements and ECMM statements. So, if at any point my questions are not clear or you just you need some time to refer to your statements, please take that. Mr. Hendriks, in response to some questions on direct examination - and I'm referring to paragraph 12 of your statement at 931 - if can you go to your statement from 2008, in paragraph 12, you note: "In my previous statement, I also stated I saw a lot of RSK soldiers in Knin and that they may have been on rotation. What I meant by this is that there were a lot of RSK -- ARSK soldiers in the town of Knin, but they were just hanging around and mainly drinking. It wasn't as if they were part of a unit." Now, shortly after you arrived in Knin, you were aware, were you not, that the HV had taken Bosansko Grahovo, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically. It's perfectly conceivable that that was mentioned, but I don't remember that specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware, Mr. Hendriks, that on the 28th of July, President Milan Martic declared a state of war on the entire territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can go to your first statement from 1996, which is D820, at the bottom of the second page of the document, and the first page, it is a fact that at the time, prior to Operation Storm, the military situation was tense, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As you said in your 2008 statement, there were a lot of soldiers in town and; also, you also noted that every military capable man was mobilised, and I think you told us on direct between 18 and 50 years of age. So, for the situation in Knin, in the latter part of July and the first days of August, everything was very tense and there was a fear of something about to happen, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you also noted that in your statement to the Prosecution, again in paragraph 12, in that last sentence: "I can confirm that I did not see any ARSK heavy artillery or tanks in and around Knin." Now, my colleague, Mr. Kuzmanovic, brought to your attention D821 which is an ECMM situation report or ECMM report for the 2nd of August, where the Kenyan Battalion reported shelling by the ARSK, at least 50 times. Now, sir, when you are saying and you told the Prosecution that you didn't see any heavy artillery, you are not saying that they didn't have the artillery; simply that you didn't see it. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, in fact, I think you told us that you were not allowed to monitor the confrontation lines prior to Operation Storm that were being held by the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, if they had artillery and tanks at the front line on the morning of the 4th of August, you simply wouldn't know about it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you also -- if I can just shift topics but say in the same vein of pre-Storm, you noted in your 1996 statement that: "Prior Operation Storm, people were ..." -- and I refer to page 2 of the statement. If I can get the exact location, it's about three quarters of the way down: "In the days before Operation Storm ..." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "In the days before Operation Storm, there a lot of rumours among the people and they became very restless, and not knowing what to do, some of them were able to leave to Serbia or Bosnia." Now, one of your -- your landlady attempted to go as well, didn't she?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And understanding that you came to the area on the 24th of July, how much prior to that did this departure of people from Knin or the area begin?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me rephrase it. It was probably not a very clear question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With the understanding that you came to Sector South on the 24th of July, approximately when did this departure of people from Knin begin?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was in the week of 31 July, perhaps the weekend before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the evacuation came in earnest after this radio broadcast on the 4th of August by the RSK authorities. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And was this -- were you familiar with the evacuation order that was signed by President Martic?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But this evacuation began -- I think you told us the evacuation began towards the eve -- on the evening of the 4th of August. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was told by the people who entered the barracks, and they said that to my interpreter. It was said that the evacuation started in the course of the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, if we can just take this chronologically from your own experience, the shelling of Knin began in the early morning hours of the 4th; and then these people told you that sometime in the afternoon, Radio Knin broadcast that the civilian population should evacuate; and then that's when the civilian authorities began to evacuate. Is that basically the progression?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's basically the progression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as part of this progression, you told us -- or, actually, is mentioned in Exhibit 820, that buses came to - and I'm looking at 820, your 1996 statement - buses came to the governmental building to pick people up and to take them away. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... told that as well.

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was told that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, after the evacuation began, you were also informed that that is when the ARSK soldiers began to leave the front lines to go back to their families. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In a sense, they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I seek clarification on one of the previous issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, in one of the questions of Mr. Kehoe the Knin Radio, could I say, call for an evacuation was put to have taken place in the afternoon; and you apparently agreed with that. Could you tell me exactly what the source of your knowledge of the radio broadcast by Radio Knin in the afternoon, on what that is based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that through the report by my witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But did your interpreter tell you that it was in the afternoon? Was any time given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm translating what it says here. So I heard from my interpreter that in the afternoon of the 4th, after an entire afternoon of broadcasting music, there was a recorded tape by Martic, stating there was no reason to panic because the defence positions were stable. So, exactly when this broadcast took place is impossible for me to say, but I suspect it was sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I may just try to find where exactly what you read. Of course, some of these statements are relatively new to us as well. So you were reading. I haven't got it in front of me at this moment. Which page is that of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we go to -- it's D820; and if we go to the top of, it's page 3 of the document. Actually, it's on the screen, Judge, if we can just scroll up just a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And we look at point 3: "The leadership in Knin was the first who fled away. From my interpreter, I learned that in the afternoon of the 4th, after a whole day of broadcasting music, a recorded tape of Martic was broadcasted with a statement that there is ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because you earlier said "From your own observation, you said ..." But I do understand that you learned from your the interpreter that it was the afternoon. I'm just trying to follow the chronology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kehoe, I am aware that I urged you to do this efficiently as possible, but sometimes I have a need to verify exactly what the basis for the question and the answer is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if Your Honour wants any additional clarification on the chronology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's clear enough. The question came to my mind when you referred to his own observation and the broadcasting in the afternoon, where I had no recollection that the witness testified that he personally observed or heard. But it is hearsay and it appears here, and that has been clarified now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think I did ask the question on the recollection. I think the witness corrected me and said "I heard it from my interpreter." So maybe I threw you off with my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your question was about chronology. So the personal observation and where the chronology came from exactly, that was on my mind. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think we left off, Mr. Hendriks, that this abandonment of the positions by the ARSK soldiers began after this notice on the radio that the civilian population should evacuate. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's perfectly possible. Perhaps, before that, some soldiers are left as well, but I think that the majority of the soldiers left after that broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just shift subjects for one moment -- for the next series of questions, Mr. Hendriks, and I want to focus just briefly on paragraph 16 of your 2008 statement, P931. And you note towards the bottom of the page, and we're talking about the artillery, that the purpose was to break the resistance of the army by having them surrender or flee and, at the same time, to scare the civilians into abandoning the area. Now, sir, as an artillery -- as an anti-aircraft officer, or retired anti-aircraft officer with the Dutch military, you know that the purpose of artillery, in part, is to break the resistance of the opposition, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would -- could be one of the duties of artillery fire, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And one of the other purposes of artillery fire could be knocking out the communication capabilities of the enemy; and by that, I mean radio, television, any other means of communicating that a military force might have. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible, depending on the priorities of the artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the shelling of Knin, you do not know whether the headquarters of the army of the Serb Krajina were, in fact, hit, do you? And I'm talking about the shelling on the 4th, on the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated at the time that most important sites and buildings were not destroyed, so probably not the headquarters of Serb Krajina army either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me, if I may, let me show you D389. And, sir, this is an intelligence report by the army of Serb Krajina from the 4th of August of 1995, and I refer you to the fourth paragraph down. Of course, this is a report by the ARSK concerning the attack on the 4th. It notes that: "Knin was attacked from Livanjsko Polje from several directions, and by the time this information was drafted between 2000 and 300 rounds of different calibres impacted on the town. The first to strike was carried out on the building of the SVK General Staff which suffered great damage ..." This is a report in evidence concerning what the ARSK reported. My question to you, sir, is: You didn't know about this. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't speak about this, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, if you speak too quickly, there is an additional problem, that is, that the interpreters will rely, more or less, on the transcript as well, just to catch up with where they are behind. Then we may have sometimes double problems: One, that the transcript is not always fully able to follow you; and, then, the interpreters relying on the transcript have additional problems. Could you please keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question -- and I apologise, sir, and to the interpreters for moving too quickly. My question to you, sir, is that when you were writing your reports, you did not know that the ARSK headquarters had been hit by artillery fire on the morning of the 4th, did you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. If we continue with this document and go to the next sentence: "Later, the fire was transferred to the military barracks, 13 Kaplara, the Tvik factory, the railway intersection, and residential buildings and the area beneath the Knin fortress." You, likewise, did not know that the military barracks had been hit, nor the Tvik factory and the railway intersection. Isn't that so, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, you didn't know they were hit?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So when you told the Prosecution in paragraph 16 of your statement - and I'm talking about 931 - that first sentence: "My observations were that shells seemed to be following everywhere and no where, and did not seem to be aimed at specific targets." You made that statement, did you not, because you didn't know what specific targets had been hit. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 16 and in general, to be quite honest, during our drive through Knin, the general observation was that large parts of those targets were still intact. It is perfectly possible that they had been hit, but then the question is what degree of destruction had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me take one step further. You just mentioned your drive through Knin when you were going to UN Sector South. Approximately what time of day was this?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around midday, around noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And during that drive through Knin, you saw no casualties, did you? I refer you to your 1996 statement, D820, in the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any injured during that ride.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if I can bring up P947, P947.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, this is a photograph that Prosecution put into evidence through you, noting that this was damage in Knin that you observed on the 12th of August of 1995. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn our attention to P62. I'm sorry, P62. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, this is an overhead of the Knin area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I would ask the assistance of the usher, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would like, Mr. Hendriks, if you could use this overhead and tell us where these buildings were that you identified as being in Knin which we just saw on P947.

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
