utterances.text: Well, I would have to take a guess, but I suspect about in this area, but I'm not sure. Because if I remember correctly, this is where the UN barracks were and that our homes were about here, and this is about how we drove. So I suspect about halfway, but it's a guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can orient you just a bit, so maybe it could be a little bit easier. If you look at the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With the assistant of the usher, could we blow up the right-hand side of the photograph, so maybe it would be easier for Mr. Hendriks to get oriented. Oh, okay. They tell me it would lose the red mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just at the right-hand side, sir, the right-hand side of the photograph there that is encircled, that is the UN barracks. My apologies to you. I probably should have done that previously. But, with all due respect, with that in mind, sir, and if you orient yourself, if you want to re-draw that with that orientation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We certainly is would have no objection to that, Judge, because I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the usher could to assist, too, if you are seeking to remove the earlier one, or should we keep it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No. I think, in fairness to the witness, Judge, if we orient him, and I think he was just a bit confused as to where the UN barracks was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But my question is whether we want the first marking to be removed and then to be replaced by it, or that we add to the original, perhaps mistaken, marking another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have no objection to removing it, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think it might be less confusing for those who will at a later time look at it. Madam Usher, could you assist the witness in removing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I just, now that it is removed, if we could zoom in on the UN barracks on the right-hand side, so that the witness could just get oriented just a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We start over again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, you may always ask to have portions being zoomed in, if that assists you in orienting yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with that orientation, Mr. Hendriks, can you tell us where this photograph that you took -- or that was taken and you identified, P947, was taken in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I would just like, pursuant to the witness's previous answer, to invite him not to guess, but, really, if he remembers where the location is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we do not expect anything less from Mr. Hendriks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't really remember. It would really boil down to guessing, but I do know that somewhere in Knin were these two buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, let me show you a series of photographs, which is 1D55-0020.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this is a series of three photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, looking at the first photo that you had, this is the photograph that you admitted into evidence, which is P947.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could then go to the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, those are the photographs of the same buildings in the same area, obviously taken after these buildings have been refurbished, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it looks like, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could go to the next photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is an overhead of the street in the previous photograph, which is in Grahovo, the street is actually Sarajevska Ilica, S-a-r-a-j-e-v-s-k-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just for reference purpose, Your Honour, this photograph is taken from -- if we could go back one photograph, just to reference ourselves. This is taken from the direction of Livanjsko Polje going into Grahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So would you agree with me, Mr. Hendriks, that the photograph you identified as being in Knin is a photograph of buildings that were -- or are located in Grahovo?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it on the condition that these are photographs taken in Grahovo. Mr. Hendriks, would you make a clear distinction between what you know and what you are, even in this courtroom, told. You have had perhaps 30 seconds to look at all this, and then you confirm that this is Knin but Grahovo. Well, I can imagine that you say, "Well, it looks very much as if it is the same, and if I thought that the first photograph was taken in Knin, and if this photograph is not taken in Knin, so I must have been made a mistake." That's all fine. But you now already have situated when have you been for the last time in Grahovo and have identified these buildings as being in Grahovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In my first statement from 1996, I attached a photograph; and then, in April 1996, I thought that the apartment buildings were Knin. That's why I said that the photograph had been taken of apartment buildings in Knin. It's possible, because there was no caption under the photograph, that I made a mistake at that time, because we didn't go to Grahovo that many times. But if this building -- these buildings could be in Grahovo, but exactly the same buildings could be in Knin, but I don't know. So I don't know whether that photograph was taken in Knin or in Grahovo. But in 1996, I thought that the photograph had been taken in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no question about that. Your testimony now is that from what you see now, that you made a mistake at that time, which, of course, is important for to us know. At the same time, I did put this question to you in order to make you aware that you apparently, as I take from your last answer, without any factual knowledge, you just now locate these buildings in Grahovo where they may well have been. I was not able to check that on the basis of Google Earth. I see "photograph of Grahovo, 2008." So, apparently, someone writes on this photograph that it was taken in Grahovo. But, apparently, you have you no knowledge of that. What you do have is a strong impression that you perhaps have made a mistake, and whether this is a Grahovo building or whether it's any other place. If you know, please tell us; if you don't know, please be more careful in answering to questions that you would agree with Mr. Kehoe that this is a building in Grahovo. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I could move into evidence 1D55-0020, the array of three photos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This issue seems to me -- I mean, of course, we could do a lot. It takes a bit to compare surroundings. It is also known that sometimes buildings are approximately the same, especially new buildings. It seems to me that this is an excellent opportunity to speak with the Prosecution and see whether they agree, which avoids that the Chamber starts analysing exactly on the basis of the photo material not having any opportunity to go beyond that, and perhaps reach conclusions, perhaps wrong conclusions, perhaps right conclusions; whereas, the parties are in a better situation to compare all information they have and to come to an agreement on whether the witness really made a mistake. Perhaps could you agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I mean, I haven't seen these before yesterday, so I'm in the same position as you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you at this moment to come to final conclusions and to agree, but it appears to me that this is by accident an opportunity to agree on a very factual issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm more than happy to discuss the foundation of this picture with Mr. Kehoe and see if we can come to an agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if you want to MFI this at the time or just take it into evidence, subject to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think, Mr. Hedaraly, can we take it into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think we can, but there's the foundation issue that you've raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, if the witness says it is Grahovo where has no knowledge of it, of course, we'll not give much weight to Grahovo, nor to 2008, nor to anything else. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D822.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D822 consists of three photographs and is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, just staying a bit with the shelling issue, I take it that -- or were you involved with any of the UN military observers who did an assessment of shelling of Knin and determined that the shelling was concentrated on military objectives? Were you involved in that or did you become aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved, but I did become aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did you learn that the assessment of the UN military observers was that the shelling of Knin was, in fact, concentrated on military targets -- or military objectives?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, generally, were you aware that that was their conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you, likewise, aware that the UNCIVPOL -- that UNCIVPOL did a similar analysis and came up with a similar result; that is, that the shelling was concentrated on military objectives?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not learn anything like that from the UNCIVPOL. We were in contact with the UN headquarters for Sector South, and that's where the military analysis came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me shift gears with you just a moment, sir, and let me take you to the period of time directly after Operation Storm. And were you aware that right after Operation Storm, north of Knin and north up through Strmica, there continued to be fighting between the ARSK and HV troops?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether that was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, maybe, were you aware at this point if any fighting was taking place north of Strmica at all after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is perfectly possible that that took place at the time, but I don't know now whether I was aware of it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if I can take you to exactly -- or ask you about some of the events transpired directly after Storm. Were you aware that on the 9th of August that General Gotovina issued an order for active defence in the confrontation line between the Serbs and the HV? Were you aware that that took place on the 9th of August?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to P830, which is an ECMM report of 10 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I could move to the second page, 3 f, towards the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This was read to you during your direct examination: "Team Knin report the continuing restriction of movement. In trying to get to Benkovac and Obrovac, they were told by the policija on the check-points they could only get to these places with written permission from General Gotovina." Do you recall, Mr. Hendriks, if there were HV troop movements during this particular area when you and other members of the Team Knin came to this check-point?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were there troop movements coming from or resupplying, if I may -- were there anybody resupplying from the coast up through this area and up to the confrontation line? Was that going on, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say, Mr. Hendriks, that at this particular time, you didn't know anything about what the HV was doing concerning troop movements, resupply, or somehow planning for the next operation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't receive that information from General Cermak or CALO, and those were our counterparts. We were not told what the HV troops were doing. That was not really our business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let me shift, if I may. And I noted in your statement - and I'm talking about your 1998 [sic] statement at paragraph 8 - that you reviewed reports before they were sent to Zagreb: "And I have never seen anything in these reports that struck me as being inaccurate or inconsistent with my observations for that day." I'd like it turn your attention to P805, and if I could go to -- and P805, just to orient you, sir, is a 7 August 1995 report by ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can go to the second page of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And on the 7th of August, ECMM reports in point b: "In the Knin area, it seems as if random looting and destruction of houses and property is about to reach a degree where it will get even more difficult to re-start normal life." Comment: "It is very unlikely that this is a deliberate policy of the authorities." Now, you agree with that, do you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the comment, ECMM comment, let me just stay at the beginning that you told us in direct and on also in your statement at paragraph 8, you have never seen anything in these reports that struck me as being inaccurate, and you noted on direct that you read these reports. And the comment here is that it says it is very unlikely that this, talking about looting and destruction of property, that this is a deliberate policy of the authorities. Now, you agree with that, don't you, sir, or this assessment made by ECMM on the 7th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant in my statement here about everything that I saw and read elsewhere, I was referring primarily to segments of text that were taken over from my own report or summarized. So I didn't mean that I always agreed with entire RC reports because that was not my responsibility; but the sections gleaned from my own team report I was curious about them, I read them, and they conveyed the truth at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this is -- this report is written by Mr. Bigland and Mr. Liborius and on behalf of RC Knin. Now, this accurately reflects the position of RC Knin on the 7th of August, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hendriks, I'm not saying that looting did not take place, but, initially, some of the searches of -- let me withdraw that. As a military man, you understand that some of the searches that were taking place in the Knin area were, in fact, done for security reasons, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn your attention to some of the reports that talk about the civilians returning to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what I'd like to do is if I could just, in the spirit of moving more quickly, Your Honour, just go through a couple of reports and then just ask a question from there. If I can turn first to P352.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This may not have been a document that you saw previously, but it is a Sector South situation report from 6th August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could go one, two, three, five pages in, if I may, or maybe six pages, yeah, six pages in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's focus on paragraph F. It reflects in the middle that: "More civilians, including cars with Split licence plates, are seen in Knin ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can go to P806 which is an ECMM report of 8 August 1995, and if I could go to second page, 4 a.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Last sentence: "DPs, displaced persons, already returning to their homes, as of the 8th of August."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: P933, which will be the last report in this series, which is a report to RC Knin of 9 August 1995 from November 2, Team N2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The last paragraph on that general situation: "It seems like Knin, for the first time, is becoming a big tourist attraction. Extensive traffic was recorded on the main road between Knin and Drnis."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the middle there: "We saw the same development in Drnis. A lot of civilians are in the city, and it seems that they are looking for property that belonged to them ..." Now, almost immediately after Operation Storm, Mr. Hendriks, the civilian population began to come back to Knin and the outlying areas to attempt to re-take their property. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think there's a vagueness to the question. Are we talking about the Croat civilians that came back that left in 1991 or during the war, or the Serbs that had left in August --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise in your question, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hendriks, were there a lot of Croat displaced people, who had been evicted from Knin between 1991 and 1995, were a lot of those Croats coming back to Knin and the outlying areas to attempt to take their property that previously belonged to them?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe they were displaced persons. You could tell that from the licence plates on the cars. But whether they were looking for their own belongs or belongings of others, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, if we look at this report, it notes that: "A lot of civilians are in the city, and it seems they are looking for property that belonged to them previously." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would, indeed, mean that they were looking for their own home to check for their belongings. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this happened almost -- and the first report that we talked about was the 6th of August. This happened almost immediately after Operation Storm, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us take that issue of the civilians coming back into the area with the situation report that my colleague, Mr. Kuzmanovic, discussed with you, which was P35, the second page under "Military assessment," where it is written that: "It is assessed that the swiftness of the success of Operation Storm ..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry, P935. My apologies. P935. My apologies, Mr. Usher. Could we go to the second page of that assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It notes, yes: "It is assessed that the swiftness of the success of Operation Storm caught not only the HV by surprise but also the civilian authorities who were supposed to go in afterward and take over. Consequently, as the capital felt in 36 hours, instead of the expected week, the military and police who were to next arrive did so late. The civilian authorities were also caught on the hop and have not been able to bring their move forward at all."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last report, which is P830, section 2 a. This is an ECMM report of 10 August 1995. It notes that: "The political authorities of Knin have still not moved in. There is no one to talk to."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hendriks, at this particular point, beginning on 6th August, there is a civilian population that is moving down into -- coming back into Sector South; the military and the civilian police have gotten in late; and ECMM reports that as late as 10 August, there is still no political authorities that have moved in and no one to talk to. Is that an accurate assessment of the situation when we combine those ideas?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's possible. I have a different impression. The Croatian troops invaded the area and then are basically in command of the area, so they might put up all kinds of check-points and other obstacles to obstruct the civilian population. Apparently, that didn't happen, but perhaps the civilian authorities were not prepared for the rapid conquest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And were you aware, Mr. Hendriks, that in -- on the 6th of August, 1995, the constitutional order of the Republic of Croatia was reinstituted in Knin and that civilian authorities took over on the 6th of August? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not, specifically, but I assumed that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the early days after Operation Storm, sir, there was a serious power vacuum in the Knin area, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that properly because we were quickly introduced to General Cermak, the military commander on site, who represented himself as being responsible for law and order throughout the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think you said in response to questions by -- by my colleague, Mr. Cayley, that General Cermak was attempting to be helpful to the ECMM and the UN, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But prior to Operation Storm, in the area, some 12.000 Croat homes had been destroyed, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean in the war in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Between 1991 and 1995, were you aware that 12.000 homes had been burned, Croat homes, prior to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that at the time there had been some damage; but whether it was 12.000 homes, I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I reference you to the testimony of Ive Kardum of last week at page 9420, line 17. It says: "As I already mentioned, there some 12.000 Croat house, Croat houses that had been burned. You, as you sit here, you were unaware of that figure. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with the knowledge that you were unaware with that figure, when you were assessing the 60 to 70 per cent of houses destroyed as a result of Operation Storm -- and I'm referring to the report of -- that was filed as P815. That would be the first page, where it notes: "It is a rough estimate that between 60 and 80 per cent of the property in the former UN Sector South have been fully or partially destroyed." When that was reported, was that reported without the knowledge that approximately 12.000 homes, Croat homes, had been burnt prior to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me just discuss the report that Mr. Hedaraly addressed to you, which is P920.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, P920.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You earlier referred to line 9490, line 17, as far as the -- that's at least what I read in the transcript. I'm there discussing with Mr. Mikulicic how much time he would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge, if I made a mistake. It should have been 9420, 9420, line 17 and 18, if I misspoke on that score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's where I am -- no, I think that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I misspoke. 9420, line 17, in my transcript, is a discussion with Mr. Mikulicic about how much time he needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is in the -- actually, it is interesting. There is an number up here, if we can turn to 9498.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I was referring to the number at the top, but it may be 9498, line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the real source, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think the reference number at the top is when the testimony actually begins, and I was reading that number as opposed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I could bring up P938.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, this is the document that Mr. Hedaraly showed to you on direct examination; and on the -- I believe he directed your attention to Polaca, P-o-l-a-c-a, which is about in section c, about one, two, three, four, five, six, or seven down, where you noted that the damage was by 1991 damage. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, so do we take it from the rest of this report that the damage in all of the rest of these villages was as a result of post-Storm activities?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a consequence of operations after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me bring up for you, if I may, D751, and turning to pages 2 and 3 of that document. And this is the villages that are listed for that date for the 22nd of August that Mr. Hedaraly referred you to, and with the clarifications that are set forth in the left. And if we could just go to the next page of this document, I'd like to just to talk to you a little bit about this. Now, just looking at that, some of these villages -- and if we look at the top, third from the left, Pridraga, which is Donja Viduka, which is on your list and you note that it is totally destroyed, and the 1991 census reflects that it is almost entirely a Croat village. Over to the lower right-hand corner, we have Lisicic, which is not an entirely a Croat village, but virtually all Croat. That is totally destroyed. If we just go up to the right just a little bit more, in Medjvida, the report reflects that is totally destroyed, and that is a mixed village with more than half being Croat. Staying with this document, if we can go to Zupane in your list, you say it is partially destroyed. That is on the left-hand side. And a partially destruction reflects it is mostly a Serb village. Rodaljice -- excuse me, I'm sorry. It is Kolarna, which is in the area of Rodaljice, which is another Croat village that is partially destroyed. Now, just staying with this, sir, based on your assessment, what were villages that were mainly Croat villages prior to Operation Storm, your reports reflect were destroyed after Operation Storm. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't get that. I don't understand the question properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just take these one by one, and maybe I moved too quickly. Look at the top, we have Pridraga, which is in the top left-hand corner, and then in parenthesis is "Donja Viduka." We have according to the 1991 census 1.770 Croats, two Serbs, and seven others. So the 1991 census reflects that this is a Croat village. Your assessment, in your report that we have reflected in this map, is that this village was totally destroyed and there's no indication that it was destroyed prior to Operation Storm. So is it your position, Mr. Hendriks, that the Croats, after Operation Storm, were destroying villages that were almost entirely Croat prior to -- well, per the census of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My perception was that villages were destroyed primarily where Serbs were in the majority, but there were also houses burned that belonged to Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, let me try to see whether I can get you on the track of Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is drawing your attention to the following: In the survey of the damage to villages, you have indicated, at least once for Polace, that this was damage pre-Operation Storm. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as, for example, Pridraga is concerned, the report does not indicate that it is pre-Operation Storm damage and describes the village as totally destroyed. Mr. Kehoe puts to you that the population of Pridraga, on the basis of the 1991 census, was by a very vast majority Croat. He now wonders whether the damage, which appears in your report, total destruction, is Operation Storm damage, which would mean that the Croats would destroy a village which was by the vast majority Croat, in 1991, during Operation Storm; that is to say, that they were destroying their own villages. That, Mr. Kehoe, if I well understood you, is the issue you wanted to raise with Mr. Hendriks. Mr. Hendriks, could you comment on this line of reasoning as a product of your report at that time and the added information of the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems unlikely to me that during Operation Storm, the Croats would completely destroy a village that, prior to 1991, was overwhelming Croat. Perhaps the survey was incomplete, but I can't say that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Incomplete in what respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That perhaps it should have indicated that the village had already been destroyed prior to 1991, but I couldn't tell that you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me just take this one step further, and if we can look at the two villages that you have toward the top. One is Zapuzane which you have undamaged; and Komazeci in the Komazeci valley, which is also untouched. If with go to the map, Zapuzane is on the left-hand side, midway down: "Nine Croats and 532 Serbs." So we could say that is virtually an entire Serb village. And if we go to the other side of the map and we go to Komazice, that is, by the 1991 census, an entirely Serb village. Your report reflects that both of those entirely Serb villages were not damaged. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if, in fact, ECMM was of the belief, as they say in 815, P815, that the destruction of these Serb homes was -- or destruction of the -- withdraw that -- that the burning that was going on was organised in some fashion, why do we find Croat villages that are totally destroyed, while in the same patrol that you took on the 22nd of August, you have Serb villages which are virtually intact? Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the damage that you are looking at and that you observed, that was coming at a time when the Republic of Croatia had a serious problem housing displaced people who were down on the coast or were in other locations, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, possible. If it is possible, let's just talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go to P935.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, can we concentrate on what the witness knows. I don't know whether -- he says this is possible. Of course, if you give him further information, he might say it is likely or the document says so. That, of course, is not the kind of testimony we are seeking at this moment. But please proceed, and keep this in back of your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Maybe it is easier, Judge, if I go through again a series of ECMM reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if you want to take a break now. I can probably shorten this up and finish relatively quickly when we come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps that could be a good idea, but I'd like to put one or two additional questions before we do so, which are the following. I have looked, Mr. Hendriks, at these photographs, not only 30 seconds but a bit more, and I looked at your statement. Let me say it cautious at this moment, there is a likelihood on the basis of the Google Earth map where it's indicated that the other picture would have been taken in Grahovo. From the Google Earth, I take it Bosansko Grahovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said you have taken this picture approximately 12th of August. Now, could you tell us when you last visited Grahovo, Bosansko Grahovo? Did you go there after Operation Storm? Did you go there prior to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were in Grahovo before Operation Storm, and I believe afterwards, again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, when you went there before Operation Storm, was there already considerable damage to that town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you went there after Operation Storm, was that town substantially damaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking this because you're producing a photograph with, well, substantial damage to the buildings shown there, and that there's a likelihood that this is a photograph taken from an apartment building in Bosansko Grahovo. Now, I'm trying to understand where, what, went wrong? Is there is possibility, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not that something's going wrong. It's -- the issue is my memory. In April 1996, I assumed that the photograph had been taken in Knin. Perhaps it turns out know that the buildings were in Grahovo. Then apparently, on 12 August, I was in Grahovo, but I don't remember anymore. That was 13 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say on the 12th of August. Your statement says it was on or around. Apparently, now you have a piece of information which focuses you exactly on the 12th of August, or is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because my first statement reads dated approximately, so about 12 August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I described on 23rd of April, 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you're now saying: "Then apparently on the 12th of August, I was in Grahovo." Is this just a deduction from what you see on the photograph because you say, "I took it; I must have been there." Is that what you're telling me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If those buildings are, indeed, in Grahovo. But the same type of buildings may have been in Knin. But if they were not in Knin, if that's concern, then this photograph was taken in Grahovo, or it could have been a different city. I can't explain that, but we were in Grahovo. So, presumably, we were in Grahovo around the 12th, and I took this photograph or my colleague, Stig Marker-Hansen, did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I may have some information that helps the Chamber. I don't want if you want to address it while the witness is present or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we will ask the witness to already take his break, and then you can address me. Could I ask Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We'll have a break of some 20 minute, approximately, Mr. Hendriks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There is a report, Your Honour, that was addressed in direct examination. It is a P934, which is an 11 August daily report. And on the second page, there's a reference to the damage in Grahovo. It's listed there in the report as damage from shelling, and I raised it with the witness because the church was undamaged. So that would seem to indicate that the witness was in Grahovo on the 11th of August. I don't know if that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where the witness earlier refers to the 12th, he earlier appeared not to be certain about whether it was the 12th or not. That could explain it. Of course, I'm asking this because, of course, I have great concerns in that, if there are made such mistakes, could it be a photograph taken by someone else who has kept the negatives, because I think it was not all electronic photographing yet. So it's a matter of exploring what seems to be mistakes and to try to understand what happened in order to be better able to assess where we should be extremely cautious in material that is produced. Have you ever asked the witness whether he still has the negative available to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I have not, Your Honour, because he said it was in Knin, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You had no reason at that time to doubt that. I think, after the break, one of the things we could do is to ask him whether he has still kept the negatives, because if that is the case, then it might further assist you in coming to agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the new photographs are taken in Grahovo - and of course, I have no reason at this moment to have any doubt about that - then it really seems that the other photograph is taken in Grahovo as well, and all kind of other details, which is, of course, of some concerns. Not that the photograph was taken, but that it is presented as Knin damage. We will have a break and resume at 1.00, and we would like to finish with the witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, a few more questions on the photograph of the damaged building. Do you still have the negatives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know where they are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps Stig Marker-Hansen has them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This one photograph, was it by chance that you had kept it, or do you have a whole series?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have several photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you shown all of them to the investigators or the members of the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've just shown this one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, the five that were attached to the first statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you be willing to make available the other photographs you still have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether the parties have any interest in looking at other photographs. Then, of course, if that's the case, we would invite the witness to tell us when they were taken, and perhaps even more important, where they were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any need for that, then we know at least that there's a source of information. How relevant, I have got no idea. But if the parties want to explore it, it is there. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, before we move off the -- the chart that's on the screen, and also looking at your list of villages that is in P938, given your answer previously, sir, it's accurate to say that you cannot tell whether the damage you observed on the 22nd of August, 1995, happened before Storm or after Storm. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for certain. But what we were looking for at the time, of course, we were looking for recently damaged and burned houses. So if the report read damaged, without stating that we could that he will it was from 1991, then it had been burned recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So staying with the village that we talked about previously, which virtually an entirely Croat village, Pridraga, which is Donja Viduka at the top of the page, which had 1.770 Croats, and you say that's totally destroyed, you don't know, as you sit here, whether that was destroyed before Storm or after Storm, do you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, just a last subject here, sir. You noted for us, in response to the questions by my colleague, Mr. Kuzmanovic, and this is at line -- excuse me, page 33 today, line 12: "From what you saw and you observed during the course of time in Sector South, it is true, is it not, that the civilian authorities, based upon what was going on in Sector South, were not prepared to deal with the problems they were facing, specifically looting and burning. Correct?" Your answer is: "I suspect that is correct." Now, if we could just briefly, quickly go through a series of ECMM reports, and I'd just like to ask you a question or two from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, going to first P935. This is an ECMM report of the 13th of August, and if we can go to the page three of this document at the bottom of the page, "Humanitarian assessment."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The second -- bottom of that page, just before it ends at paragraph: "DPs," displaced people, "from hotels, caravan sites along the coast, and refugees from Western Europe, have been seeping back to visit their original homes, (some to stay). Representative of Split Zupanja, DPs association estimates 100.000 DPs will return to free territories?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could go to P511, this is an ECMM report of 18 August, and if we could go to the second page, "The Economic infrastructure."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of that page: "Today the rain and the sheer lack of unburned houses meant that few fires were observed. And the lack of unburned houses meant that few fires were observed. The fields are still left with nobody working in them. How the Croatians will harvest the crops is not yet known. It seems to become a large problem, or will they just rotten in the fields? Will the DP become forced labour in the fields?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Next, just to 20 August 1995, which is P937, another ECMM report, and if we can go to the last page, which is under "Humanitarian assessment," 3 d.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "DPs and refugees from Croatia and Europe are filtering back into the area; however, no infrastructure and destroyed houses make immediate habitation possible."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: P812, 23 August 1995, under the political station. If we can just scroll down just a bit, under: "The plan..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "The plan for B," being Benkovac, "is to serve as accommodation to DPs coming from the tourist areas. These will be accommodated in tents, if necessary."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to P3 -- 953, which is the last document. This is 9 October 1995, and if we can go to the economic matters on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a discussion between the Team Knin: "Meet the manager of the screw factory Tvik in Knin," and there's a discussion, you can read it, about ECMM assisting at Tvik factory. Towards the bottom of that paragraph, it notes: "Team comment, TC: 'Housing problem is paramount. Nobody will come to work without this problem solved.'" Now, sir, my question, based on those reports, is that ECMM saw that this burning was causing a tremendous problem for the Republic of Croatia because it was preventing displaced people from coming back into the area. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you would agree with me that while this burning was going on, it did not serve the interests of Croatia -- of the Republic of Croatia because it prevented these displaced people from coming back to their homes or inhabiting other homes. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Houses that had been set on fire could obviously not be occupied by displaced persons; but in the cities, a lot of houses had not been set on fire, and then the question was simply which house do we allocate to whom? So there was a housing problem. On the one hand, there were some houses available to put people in, but it had to be authorised; but houses that had been set on fire, that was a problem because you can't occupy those for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, we saw, based on the P953 that we have on the screen, that there wasn't enough housing in Knin for the workers to work at the Tvik factory. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not one on one. So there were homes, but people would move into those who were not entitled to move into them, so it was rather disordered. There was no organised procedure for who was to allow live where; and as long as it was so disorganised, fewer people came to Knin to join in that mess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was chaotic, wasn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That housing problem was chaotic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... make is that - and, of course, this is not the first time that the matter is raised - that burning houses would prevent them for being used for those who were in need of houses, then the point is made, that this may have been in the interest -- not burning, in this respect, would not have served the interests of Croatia at that point is perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My last couple of questions for you, Mr. Hendriks, has to do with your report, which is P951, which is your report concerning churches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in that church -- that list of churches, I don't see Knin. Do you know what happened to the Catholic church in Knin? This is prior to Operation Storm. Do you know what happened to the Catholic church in operation -- in Knin, prior to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The fact is that most of the churches that were preserved throughout Sector South were Orthodox churches, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't assert that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us look at P -- the last of the documents, P934.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could go to -- this is an ECMM report of 11 August 1995, and if we could go to the third page, which is 3 G.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At the bottom, Team Knin, 3 g: "Team Knin reports the churches in Polace and Vrlika, Orthodox, undamaged; but the Catholic church in Vrlika recently destroyed and with Serb graffiti on the wall." Comment: "Team had interviewed Serb refugees in the camp who were from that area, and they said that the church was untouched when they had left after shelling had started. They believed that the damage may have been done by the HV in order to put the blame on Serbs. This seems fairly sensible as it is unlikely that people fleeing for their lives would stop to write nasty messages on the wall." Mr. Hendriks, this was your team. Was it seriously the position of the team that the HV destroyed their own Catholic church in Vrlika?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have no further questions question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Hedaraly, is there any need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour. If I can have D820 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hendriks, this is your 1996 statement, a statement about which you were asked a few questions, and I want to clarify a matter in there. I don't have if have you a hard copy if front of you, but I would like to go to the third page of that document, page 2 of the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we can focus on the top part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, you were asked questions about item 3, where it says: "From my interpreter, I learned that in the afternoon of the 4th, after a whole day of broadcasting music, a recorded tape of Martic was broadcasted with a statement that there is no reason to panic because the defence positions are stable." Now, I want to move to item 4 which is in the next paragraph. It says: "Most of the RSK defence forces pulled out after the recommendation of the Krajina authorities by radio Knin to the population to flee asap in order to assist the families to escape Krajina." Now, it seems to me, and I am asking you, were there two messages that you were told were broadcast on the radio, the first one saying that defence position was stable, and second one saying that the population should leave?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were two separate broadcasts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: When you read item 3 and 4 in your statement, you wrote that. So reading it again, does it seem like you're talking about the same message or about two different messages?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then it appears to be about the same message.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So, in the same message, in 3, it says that the defence positions are stable. It also says that the people should leave.

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me read over paragraph 3 again first. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, take your time.

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in paragraph 3, it reads that a radio broadcast had been inserted, and the friend of my interpreter who was in the army heard something and talked about that, and refugees in the camp reported things as well. So this account is basically based on three sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that's an account of number 3 in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Numbers 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. If we can go to your 2008 statement now, I want to direct to paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: P931. I'm just going to wait until everyone has it on their screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And this is when you describe the state of the town on the 7th of August when you leave the UN compound, and you say: "I saw a lot of personal goods, such add clothing, furniture, and so on, thrown out of the houses and buildings in the yards. My own house was looted, and my watch, radio player, cassette recorder, and other items were missing when I returned home." Now, Mr. Kehoe asked you, at page 56 of the transcript: "As a military man, you understand that some of the searches that were taking place in the Knin area were, in fact, done for security reasons, were they not?" And you said: "Yes." And my question for you is: What you saw in town on the 7th, with all these goods in the street, did that seem consistent to you with security searches?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I have no more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I may have a few questions, but I'm first seeking information from Mr. Kehoe. You asked the witness during his ride he saw --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- casualties, yes. You referred to D820, last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 2, yes. That is missing then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you go down a paragraph, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I have page 2, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's, actually, page 3 of the document, page 2 of the statement. They're page natured differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me first read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Midway through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One short question on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked about casualties. You said, "I didn't see any injured people." May I take this to include that you didn't see any dead persons?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is also in view of this paragraph in your statement. Could we have P952 on the screen. If the parties could assist me, on what page I find the question -- let me just see. Could the parties assist me. There was a question put in relation to the persons who will be hesitant to take -- to occupy the houses that was left by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Section 5 on page 2, Your Honour, in the middle of that, section a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we enlarge that portion. It is the portion about the 453 flats, Mr. Hendriks. At the end of this subparagraph, I find the words, "Slobodna Dalmacija." I would like to know what that means for the reporting. I know that Slobodna Dalmacija is a newspaper. Now, what does it mean, that the name of this newspaper appears under this paragraph 5 a?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the entire paragraph 5 a is a translation of what was published in that newspaper on that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Some questions were put to you in relation to redistribution of livestock. Did you observe livestock which was dead and apparently not had died to the extent you could see that from natural causes?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one pig.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Is there any need to put further questions to the witness. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, Mr. Kuzmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, this concludes your testimony in this court. [Interpretation] Thank you very much for coming and for answering all questions from parties and from the Judges. Ordinarily, I add that I particularly appreciate somebody having come from so far away, but that would not be entirely appropriate. Nonetheless, I wish you a safe trip home. Thank you very much. [In English] Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Hendriks out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, There is one housekeeping matter. I had tendered 65 ter 2821 from the bar table, but our colleagues from the Cermak Defence kindly informed us that another version of that document was already into evidence under P258. So I will withdraw the request to tender 2821, and just so the record knows that P259, my apologies, is the right exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, was a number already provisionally assigned to it, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It was not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was not. Then we don't have to take any action. The withdrawal is on the record. Are there any other procedural matters because I do understand there is no witness available for the next 11 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other procedural issue to be raised? If not, then we'll adjourn. We will adjourn until Wednesday, the 1st of October, 9.00 in the morning, in Courtroom --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one issue. I note that it's a subject near and dear to your heart, but it has to do with the excerpts of the Sekulic book. I don't know if you want me to put it on the record exactly what the parameters of that was, or if you want me to do it some other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I may, I was just about to say in which courtroom we would resume, but since I have not done that yet, the adjournment is not complete. You have greed with the Prosecution about the context pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We would then have in evidence what pages you are tendering?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is 1D01-0005, which is D777; and 1D01-0001 is D813.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you will understand that is now entirely clear to me what is in evidence and what is not in evidence. Mr. Hedaraly, I take it that you'll check on what is uploaded, whether no mistakes were made, because that's the worst I could think of. Then, of course, the Chamber will know exactly which portions of the book are now tendered, and I think we admitted the portion you focussed on but we wanted to get rid of a lot of extra pages, which you were not focussing on. Which means, that I give it another chance, that we resume on Wednesday, the 1st of October, 9.00, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of October, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.36 p.m.,
